Oh, no. They refused to share the platform with me. That was their privilege of course, but I was a little curious to know the reason. The Address-Mr. Jaques
the communists, which they claim they do, they must have supported me. They were nicely on the spot, and that is how they saved their faces.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I think the answer is that they would have been wasting their time to attend.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You waste plenty of it here. As a matter of fact last session I said you were fellow travellers and I have not heard anything since-in fact, everything I have heard and seen from that day to this only proves it to the hilt.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You are wrong.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am not wrong, and I can prove it. Let the C.C.F. show me one policy on which they have not agreed with the communists.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You would not understand.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I understand too much for you, my hon. friend. The C.C.F. were on the spot at that meeting. If they had put in an appearance they would have had to support the communists against me, or they would have had to oppose the communists and support me. I answered questions that the communists at that meeting put to me for one hour and forty-five minutes. They asked me questions about butcher Franco, Mihailovich, and so on. I was asked, how did I explain my defence in this house of butcher Franco? My answer was this. I do not defend butcher Franco or butcher anybody else, but I do defend the right of the Spanish people to manage their own affairs and settle their own problems just as I defend the right of us Canadians to settle our own affairs without interference from outside. Speaking of butcher Franco, I said, "He may be a butcher. I do not know. But if he is, he is only a retail butcher." I said that the communist boss is in the wholesale butcher business and desires to have a world monopoly of butchering and fellow-travellers are only too anxious to help him to get into that position.
Then there was Mihailovich, whom I defended, I am proud to say, in this house last summer as soon as he was captured. I would recommend to hon. members a book by David Martin called "Ally Betrayed", which goes into che whole case of Mihailovich. I should like to quote from the foreword by Rebecca West, the novelist:
They lied, and knew they lied. Never was there such a debauch of lying as the communist campaign against Mihailovich; and nearly the whole of the left wing, communist or not, opened its poor silly mouth and S3166-15
swallowed the revolting mass. I am a socialist. But I have to admit that in the last few years the left wing has shown itself just about as good a custodian of the sacred principle of liberty, fraternity, and equality, as the watchdog who was found holding a lamp in his mouth for the burglar who was cracking the safe. They should have recognized this campaign for what it was. and should have realized that the men who carried it on were as likely to give the people political and economic freedom as A1 Capone and John Dillinger.
There is one other book I might recommend to hon. members if they have not read it, namely, "Animal Farm", by George Orwell. It is a small book but a masterpiece of satire.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: A very good story.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I only hope that every hon. member will read it. It is a book which could be read as a fable by children and as a satire by their parents and grandparents.
The hon. member for Peace River suggested that parliament should set up a committee to examine into un-Canadian activities to correspond with a similar committee of congress which has done a most excellent piece of work. I hope that that suggestion will be acted upon. If it is I shall be only too glad to appear as a witness and testify before it. I have nothing to hide.
The other day somebody sent me a copy of "The Nation", which is a United States leftist, fellow traveller paper. I should say that it is communist; I do not know what else you can call it. It contains an article by Carey McWilliams, called "The Cross and the Circle". I may say that the Cross and the Circle is the symbol which we Social Crediters use on our literature. He devotes most of his article to an attack on the Quebec Social Credit movement or the Union des Electeurs. He tries to prove, of course, that they are fascist and anti-Semitic. He condemns me for my association with the Christian nationalists and he says:
Although they have been asked by the leaders of Canadian Jewry on numerous occasions to repudiate Jaques, officials of the Social Credit movement of Alberta have thus far declined to do so. Jaques. they reply, "is a sick man . . . he has heart disease . . he may die any moment."
It is comforting to know that, and I can only hope that I can say with Mark Twain on a somewhat similar occasion, the report is somewhat exaggerated. But whether it is exaggerated or not, whether I die in the next minute or not, so long as I am a member of this house I intend to defend the rights, privileges and the freedom of the Canadian people, and I do not intend to be silenced by any red network, by any agent of the antidefamation league or by any other racket,

The Address-Mr. Mclvor

because that is what they are, communist rackets. I am going to fight communism so long as I have the strength to stand up and fight.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a great many things for which we are grateful. First, I am sure we are grateful that we are living and are in good health. We send our thanks to Him whom Mr. Speaker addresses respectfully every day. I vwas thankful, too, that the speech from the throne contained references to the old age pensioners. I was grateful for that because I am one who knows something of the condition under which many of the old pensioners live, and I am convinced that if this government is in power long enough some day it will pay $50 a month to the old age pensioners. I do not think that would be even enough. To my way of thinking, the pension schemes of Canada should all be united' under one head, railway pensioners and all other pensioners. They should be made compulsory and contributory because we know that there are men who earn big money and they get rid of it very easily. If they had to save to take care of their old age it would be a great benefit to them. I have known railway workers who had served to within one or two months of receiving a pension but did not get any, and I have felt that that is not fair.
Amongst railroad workers there is an organization which is advocating a contributory national pension, and I think the government will give it kindly consideration. I should like the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) to take notice of a group of civil service workers who served in the last war but who were not members of the civil service until after the war was over. These men and women, especially men, because there were not very many women in the last war, should have their cases considered1 and should get credit for the time they risked their lives overseas.
Yesterday I was pleased1 to hear the Minister jf Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) give expression to public policy in reply to a criticism from the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart). The government is well advised to be alive to the needs of Canada and to the opportunities of securing splendid people who are willing to come here and who would make good' citizens.
I had a little trouble in getting affidavits' to try to get a young man out from Belgium who fought in the Polish army against Germany, who was taken prisoner and escaped, which shows that he had a lot of initiative and would take a lot of risk. Then he fought in the Russian army against Germany. After the war
[Mr. Jaques.l
was over, he was sent back to his own home in Poland. When he went back he could not find the address of any of his kith and kin; his father, mother, uncles, aunts, brothers and sisters were all murdered. tHe was even- denied a place to call his own, even the place on which his house was built when it was destroyed. That man would make a grateful citizen of Canada and I am thankful that now he will qualify.
I am sure we were glad to see the widening of the Immigration Act to include others. I have had a plea sent to me that the citizens of India should have the same opportunity as the citizens of other countries should have when they come to Canada from Europe or from any part of the commonwealth of nations. I believe they should be treated in the same way.
As an Indian chief, Mr. Speaker, I think the Indians of Canada are entitled to become citizens of Canada. There is nobody who has any better right to become citizens of Canada than the Indians, and they will make good ones. I taught in an Indian school; I served on church committees where Indian relationships were discussed, and I have found the Indians, boys and girls, men and women, willing to cooperate with those who were willing to help. I think it is high time that the government granted our Indians the rights of citizenship.
I would be remiss in my duty if I did not say something about the Thunder Bay district. We have two progressive cities there. I think the resources of the Thunder Bay district excel the resources of any other district of the same size in Canada.
Farmers in this house know we have a splendid farming district that produces *well. We have perhaps the greatest potato yield in Canada. Our potatoes are good, even better than those that come from the maritimes. We have a 500-bushels-to-the-acre club, and I should like to know how many members in this house can say that there are farmers in their districts who can go over 600 bushels to the acre. This productivity is due in part to the energetic efforts of the farmer representatives of our community and of our agricultural sub-station.
We have also fishing. Of course it does not compare with the fishing industry on the Atlantic or the Pacific, but if any of you have ever tasted lake Superior trout you will not want fish from any other place. It has a taste all its own and when you get one bite it calls for another.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It's your last.

The Address-Mr. Melvor

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I heard a man. in a public meeting at Fort William declare that we could take care of a great deal of the unemployment of Canada if our natural resources and our lumbering industry could be developed. Take our mining. It is growing, and since the United States need iron ore they will be coming to the Thunder Bay district for it. While Steep Rock is in the neighbouring constituency it is close to us, and there you get the finest grade of hematite ore produced on this continent. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) will support me, I believe, when I say that the Steep Rock mine is producing in such a way as to command the respect of all mining interests in Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And the United States.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Thank you. I knew you
had sense in your head. But we do not like to see our iron ore shipped from the head of the lakes because we have a great deal of power. We have the finest water system in Canada. The Fort William water system is half way up Mount McKay, which is 1,400 feet above sea level. Our water works are efficient, pumping clean, pure water, and it does not cost us anything to distribute that water throughout the city. There is nothing better in Canada. We have enough to attract people and induce them to come and invest their money there and develop our iron ore, but what we need is a little more consideration for the mining industry and for the development of our gold, silver, lead, copper and iron ore.
These are our outstanding needs at the present time if we are to stimulate the mining industry. When speaking of the special needs at the head of the lakes, I would mention one outstanding necessity and that is hospitalization. Our hospital is more than crowded and we shall have to build an addition to it, which perhaps will be accomplished in 1948.
We are appealing to the dominion government because about ten per cent of the beds that will be occupied will be occupied by the Department of Veterans Affairs and by the Indians. I think all hon. members will agree that there is great need for hospital construction throughout Canada. When you find that the wives of young veterans have their little bundles from heaven delivered in the hallways it is time we woke up to the needs in connection with hospitalization. The coming of these happy bundles from heaven has increased in Ontario by 111 per cent since 1939. Surely to goodness, we have enough 83166-15J
resources in Canada to take care of their arrival so that they will have a peaceful coming and a thorough upbringing.
We need to develop the waterfront, and I am sorry that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) is not at present in the chamber. In 1935 we were promised a big breakwater. It did not come and it has not come yet, though I can almost hear the waves washing against it right now. We have there a sawmill that is employing at least 500 people and it is growing every day, but that sawmill needs protection for its approach on the waterfront of Lake Superior so that extra money and time and labour will not be necessitated.
We need to open up the trans-Canada highway. It is not generally known even in this house that there are wonderful beauty spots at the head of the lakes. I was west this year when I heard a great deal about the glories and the beauties of British Columbia all along the line, but there are no finer sights to be seen than those which you can view from Mount McKay or the Port Arthur park. You will see nothing in the west that will compare with the beauties at the head of the lakes, and it would be well for the wise men of the east to come to Fort William and Port Arthur and enjoy the beauties there.
We also need a great waterways development and we thing it will come. This would enable businessmen to have their goods delivered into the very hub of Canada at cheap rates, and when this waterways development takes place the people of Canada will realize what we have there.
Another thing we need is a trade school. We have a trade school under the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) and it did a great job for our young veterans. Now we know what they are capable of doing in a trade school. I suggest that every last unemployed man in Canada should be sent to a trade school so that he may use his hands and his head in order that when his period of unemployment ends he will be better fitted for a job. I am sorry I cannot enlarge on that at the moment.
Another thing we need is still more consideration on the part of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for those who gave unselfish service during the last war. I do not need to mention the Red Cross workers because their achievement was outstanding. I would also mention the dry canteen, where women served day and night to
The Address*-Mr. Mclvor

make things comfortable and cheerful for our young men visiting the head of the lakes. We had two bands, one Scotch and one that thought it was even better. Whether it was or whether it was not is a question, but these two bands gave outstanding service day and night, sometimes at three, four or five o'clock in the morning. Their services were appreciated, and those of the people who had charge of those workers serving coffee and refreshments continually when a train came in deserve some recognition. But even better than that, I say that the Minister of National Defence should take into consideration the citizens in the different countries of Europe who protected our boys at the risk of their own lives. I know of one boy who was housed in a home where there were six children and a widowed mother. It was a big farm, at one time there was a German officer housed there and of course it was very difficult for them to hold that Canadian in confinement. Naturally, he wanted to clean up on the German, but it would not have been a good thing to do. I think a citizen of that type who has risked his or her life, the lives of his family, his home and everything, should have some recognition from this government.
I have a resolution on the order paper, but I do not think it will come up so that I shall have an opportunity to speak on it before the first of June. That is in connection with the acoustics of this chamber. I would say that it would perhaps not cost anything for a megaphone to be placed on your chair, Mr. Speaker, one in front of the Clerk, one in front of the Prime Minister, one in front of the other leaders and perhaps one to be provided) for each group, in order to try them out. We are not so conservative in this house, are we, that we are not willing to try a thing out and see if it will work? I think megaphones are an outstanding need. Nearly eleven years ago I presented a petition to the then Minister of Public Works in this respect, but it fell by the way side, and I think it is time this suggestion is taken into consideration. Surely one of the electric appliance companies or perhaps the C.B.C. would lend us enough megaphones to try them out and see how they work.
I should like to speak about housing. I visited a good many of our wartime houses in three days. I saw over 100 at one time, and I did not find anybody who wanted to move out; they were well satisfied. According to the facts that come to me now, a number of the people who have lived in those houses since they were put up, want to buy them, but they IMr. Mclvor.]
find that they are worth more now than when they were put up. I would say, and say with emphasis, that there is not a man in Canada

and we have the best brains in Canada, I suppose, in this house-and there is not a man in this house that could have done a better job in dealing with housing than the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe).
The Prime Minister was speaking about the great changes that were taking place. Of course we who took mental and moral science know that you cannot even step into the same river twice in the same place, that everything is changing and changing for the better. When we were at school we memorized the seven wonders of the world; you remember the pyramids of Egypt, the hanging-gardens of Babylon, the temple of Diana, and so on. The Minister of Reconstruction would not put one of those up against the great things of today. Compare the pyramids of Egypt with the atomic bomb as a wonder. Compare the hanging-gardens with an aeroplane containing fifty people rising from the ground under its own power. Compare the temple of Diana with some of the great wonders you see around you, like the radio. You cannot sit down to the radio and not wonder how it is that you can pick out one programme from a thousand, hear it and understand it when it is in your own language. It is one of the wonders of the world. But, Mr. Speaker, the greatest wonder of the world to me is the organization that can take a man who has gone to the devil, is down and out, and can make him clean and fit for life in society again. I would say that this parliament and this house should encourage those workers, no matter to what branch of the church they belong, to stick to their jobs. They have the greatest job in the world, and to me it is the greatest wonder in the world that a man can again be made clean, fit and whole.
I should be very remiss as an athlete-and I still try to do a little in the way of athletics even though old age may be creeping on-if I did not pay my tribute to a little girl- whether she is Scotch or not, I do not know, but her name is Scott, Barbara Ann Scott- who led all Europe in the recent skating competition. Those hon. members who skate a bit know that there is no more graceful physical exercise than skating. Swimming compares favourably with but does not excel skating, which is graceful, pleasant and develops the whole body. This little Canadian girl from Ottawa has given leadership to the boys and girls of Canada to get out of things of a questionable nature and into something that

Peace Treaties
will develop their bodies. As one of those who are fond of athletics, I want to pay my tribute to Barbara Ann Scott, and to wish her all success in the future.
On the motion of Mr. Adamson the debate was adjourned.
